newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco urges big turnout in local elections.
newsitem.headline: Morocco urges big turnout in local elections.

text.p: Morocco's dozen political parties and thousands of independent candidates moved into the last lap of campaigning on Thursday, urging voters to turn out in force for Friday's local elections.
"Participation in the polls of June 13 is a right, a duty and a responsibility," M'hamed Boucetta, leader of the old-guard opposition Istiqlal party, said.

A total of 13 political parties, including five opposition groups and around 15,000 independent candidates, are competing for 24,353 communal and municipal seats in the country's 16 provinces, including four in the disputed Western Sahara.

"Tomorrow will be a decisive turning point for political change and democratic progress...It will also be a choice for new management in the country's communal councils," said Ali Yata, a veteran politician and head of the former communist Progress and Socialism Party (PPS).
Pro-government parties have dominated parliament and local councils for about three decades and the opposition has consistently accused the administration of manipulating the results.
Last year, King Hassan pledged to throw his weight behind clean elections, saying he was fed up with the charges of vote-rigging which tarnished Morocco's image.

More than 13 million voters are expected to elect 1,547 communal (countryside area) and municipal councils which later this year will be responsible for electing a majority of members in a new upper house of parliament.
Party slogans have focused on issues like unemployment, justice, education and better management of local resources.

"We call on citizens to participate massively on Friday...Our objective is to struggle against unemployment and try to bring young people into Morocco's political and economic activity," said Ahmed Osman, leader of the Independent National Rally (RNI).

Osman, a former prime minister and brother-in-law of King Hassan, is expected to play a key role through his party in the future government coalition after the legislative elections in October, said one Moroccan political analyst.

The local elections are the first of a series which will culminate in parliamentary elections in September, with a new bicameral parliament being inaugurated by King Hassan on the second Friday of October.

The lower house of parliament will be directly elected through universal suffrage. Local councils will elect three-fifths of the members of a new upper house being set up under a new constitution approved in a referendum last September.
The upper house will have power to vote a no-confidence motion in the government and could topple it.
